title: TA8-23498
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXX XXX (herein "the claimant"), seeks refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA).
The allegations for the claimant were those included in his Personal Information Form2 (PIF).

The claimant's sister was a member of an underground Christian house church in their home area in Fujian province of China. In XXXX, 2003 she convinced him to attend the church. He was only able to attend the church on an irregular basis because he was otherwise busy XXXX. However, in 2004 the government discovered the sister's church and she was forced to leave the area and go to the USA, where she successfully sought asylum protection.

After his sister left the area, the claimant did not attend any church for quite some time. Firstly, because he was usually XXXXXX, secondly, because the Public Security Bureau (PSB) often came to the family home to look for the sister, and, thirdly, because he did not know how to find another church.

Then in XXXX, 2008 the claimant was introduced to another underground church by his friend and started to attend. However, the claimant was caught by the PSB on XXXX, 2008 when he was on his way home after the church service. They released him the next day after he had signed a document promising not to practice illegal activities again. Nevertheless, he decided to continue attending the same church, but was again caught by the PSB on XXXX, 2008 when he was acting as a lookout for the church service. This time he was detained for fifteen days and was forced to pay a fine. When he was released he was warned that any further arrest would result in serious consequences.
His parents were very afraid for him, so they made arrangements for him to leave China. He arrived in Canada on XXXXXX, 2008. Since arriving here he has joined in church services in the Toronto area.
I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. ANALYSIS Identity

The claimant's identity as a citizen of China, and of Fujian province in particular, has been established by his evidence and by his identity documents, specifically, by the certified true copy of his Chinese Resident Identity Card (RIC), and Household Register or Hukou, as tendered into evidence.3 CREDIBILITY CONCERNS

The claimant was asked how often he had attended church in 2003 and 2004. He said he had not gone very often, perhaps once a month for a total of six or seven times. Since he was not present when any members of that church were arrested he did not know any details. I asked him if the PSB had been looking for him as a result. He said that they did not come to look for him, but he had avoided them by going away to a neighbour's home.
After his sister left the area, the claimant said that he continued private religious activity by reading his Bible and praying at home.

When he found another house church through a friend in XXXX, 2008, he was again able to attend with other underground house church Christians. There were about twelve persons in the congregation. The claimant attended almost weekly, over the months from XXXX to XXXX. He did not go if he was ill or was XXXX. He noted that his income from XXXX decreased between 2004 and 2008 because there are XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.

He said that in XXXX, 2008 he was stopped by the police patrol with two other Christians after they left the church service. The police searched his bag and found Bibles, so they suspected underground Christian membership. All three were detained overnight, questioned by the PSB, and then released after they signed documents promising not to practice further illegal activities.

I asked the claimant why his original PIF narrative dated and signed on December 19, 2008 stated that he was caught by the PSB when he was attending a service,4 but at the start of his oral hearing on November 12, 2010 he amended the wording to indicate that he was caught when on his way home from the service. He answered that it was because he still was not at home, and in his view to be on his way home was considered to be part of the church activities. I do not accept his explanation as reasonable. One is either at the service or not. The location of the arrest by PSB is an important point in the account. In my view the plain language of the original narrative is inconsistent with the revision, and he failed to adequately explain this.

I asked him why his PIF narrative did not mention that there were any other persons with him when he was arrested, whereas his oral testimony was that two others were with him and were also detained, to which he replied that he thought the story was concerning himself. I pointed out to him that the instructions which preface the PIF narrative ask him to refer to "similarly situated persons." He said that he did not know of these instructions. The claimant appears to have had benefit of competent counsel, as named in his PIF signed in December 2008, throughout the hearing process. This is an important inconsistency for which he failed to give any reasonable explanation.

I also noted to the claimant that his signed declaration,5 which he wrote in his own handwriting when he first made his refugee claim on November 30 2008, stated; "on the evening of XXXX, 2008, I went as usual to a worship gathering. During that meeting, a few public security officers took me and some others away" (emphasis added). In response, he said that when he wrote his story before, he did not explain himself well due to his limited education. While I note that the claimant only attended, but did not complete Grade 10, the wording of this declaration is very clear. I do not understand why he would write down that the PSB arrested him during the meeting, if the more recent evidence he gave was that the arrests occurred when people had left and were making their way home.

In my view these are important discrepancies or inconsistencies in his testimony about his personal and direct problems with PSB. I do not find his explanations about the inconsistency as to the location of his arrest, or the number arrested with him to be a reasonable or persuasive. The claimant has had benefit of representation by competent and experienced legal counsel throughout the process of his refugee claim, and counsel was named in his PIF which he signed on December 19, 2008. Moreover, he had almost two years from that date until the November, 2010 hearing to make any amendments to this PIF narrative, but he failed to do so until the actual hearing. I therefore draw a negative credibility inference as a result of all the foregoing concerns.

I asked him about the interview with the PSB, particularly if they referred to his sister's situation in questioning him in 2008. I noted my specialized knowledge as a Refugee Protection Division member, that many claimants whose family members had previous problems with the PSB found that those issues arose again in the context of any further detention or questioning by the authorities in China. Indeed, for example, the documentation with reference to the Falun Gong Practitioners suggests that immediate family members who are themselves uninvolved may suffer various problems.6 I was puzzled that if his sister had been forced to flee the area as a wanted person because of her underground church activity in 2004, which was a few years before the claimant's problems, and he was held overnight for further interrogation by the PSB, why the authorities did not consider his sister's situation in assessing that of the claimant. The claimant responded that that was his sister's case, that his was different, and they were both grown adults.

In my experience this is not the case in China. The PSB very often take the family background of a suspect into account, and the accusation of "bad family background" or landlord class in China has only recently begun to recede with the rise of market economics. If his sister had indeed been discovered as being involved in an illegal religious organization in 2004, and forced to leave the country to make an asylum claim in the USA, I do not think it credible that the PSB would have ignored this in assessing the claimant's case.

I conclude, on the balance of probabilities, given these important and unexplained inconsistencies and implausibilities, that the PSB did not arrest him or any church attendees on XXXX XX or XX, 2008, as he has alleged.

Furthermore, I note that his Declaration,7 which he wrote when he first arrived at Pearson International Airport in Toronto, made no mention that he was involved in any further church activities after the initial detention on XXXX, 2008. His explanation as noted above with reference to another issue for the same form was that when he wrote his story before, he did not explain himself well due to his limited education. However, the Declaration states that after his first release "At the time I thought the matter was settled and everything would be fine."8 It does not say, as his PIF or oral testimony did, that he did not keep his promise to the authorities, or that he went back to the church as a lookout, or on any basis. This is also a significant omission from the Declaration compared to his PIF as it is the apparent cause of his second alleged arrest on XXXX, 2008.

I asked him why the Declaration made no mention of his sister's problems as an underground house church member. He said that he only thought to mention his own problems, and he was not very good at expressing himself. Again, if his sister had truly faced arrest and been forced to flee China, this would be an important consideration given she lived with the clamant at the time and allegedly introduced him to religion. I draw another negative credibility inference from this important omission.

I asked him if any further problems happened after he was released from detention on XXXXX, and before he left China in late XXXXX. He said that two or three weeks later, after his release, the church organizer had phoned his mother to warn her that a similar situation or PSB raid had happened to another underground church. Again I noted to him that this was not in his PIF narrative, and asked why not. He said that he only wrote simple reasons.

Once again he omitted important information pertaining to similarly situated persons, despite clear instructions in his PIF narrative. Absent any reasonable explanation, I draw a further negative credibility inference.

When I asked him if he had any recent news about his claim, he said that his mother had advised him that the PSB came to re-arrest him in XXXXX 2009 as other underground church members had been re-arrested and sentenced to two to three years. Counsel said that it was her policy to include only information to the date the PIF was first signed. That noted, I believe that it is a significant omission which should have been sent to the Board by an addendum to the narrative as soon as it came to the claimant's attention. The original narrative would lead one to believe that he did not face such an immediate risk of detention or arrest when he left China, but the additional information suggested that he was now a wanted person being sought as soon as he might return to China. The original narrative suggested that he may be arrested if he were involved in any more illegal activities; the new information is that he will be arrested as soon as he arrives back in the country. I draw a negative inference.

Moreover, as the analysis of underground church conditions and risk in Fujian below will demonstrate, I have no credible or trustworthy evidence that such detentions or sentences occur in Fujian, and certainly not for mere church members or attendees.

I asked him if he knew how many times the PSB had been to his home to look for him or arrest him since he had fled in 2008. He said that he could not recall with certainty. I repeated the question, asking if it was five or ten times, but he said that he really could not recall. His mother had only told him in telephone calls that the PSB had been to look for him again. I expected that, even taking into account his education and background in China, he should have been able to remember an approximate numerical range if the PSB were looking for him between 2009 and 2011, as this would be clear evidence about the intensity of their interest in him. He could not even hazard an approximation, so I draw a negative inference.

The claimant said that the PSB had been visiting his home to look for him a number of times since XXXX 2009, two and half years before his most recent oral hearing. There has not been any arrest warrants/summons left with his family. The documentary evidence9 states: ...it is very common in China for the police authorities to leave a summons or subpoena with family members (or possibly close friends, though that is probably less common), instructing them to pass it along to the person named on the summons. The person accepting the summons would be expected to sign an acknowledgement of receipt. This is not actually the proper procedure, but it happens all the time, especially in cases when the person on the summons is not easily locatable...[S]ome police officers themselves are not well versed in the proper procedures, and probably think that this is a perfectly acceptable practice (while others may simply be too idle to chase the person down, and rely on the public's sense of intimidation to do their work for them).

Other documentation10 highlights that the PSB rarely uses arrest warrants. The Procuratorate will issue an arrest warrant after the PSB has investigated the case and has evidence that the suspect has committed the crime. Further: ...China is still far from complying with rule of law standards. Chinese local authorities sometimes detain people or otherwise subject them to punitive measures in a way which is not in accordance with Chinese law. Similarly, some areas of China follow practices which do not conform with national laws and regulation. The Information Request above also noted that statues on arrest warrants and summonses specific to Guangdong, Fujian and Liaoning could not be found among the sources consulted by the Research Directorate.

Although the documentary evidence is mixed, it is reasonable to conclude that the authorities have concluded some investigation which gives rise to them stating that he was identified as being involved in illegal religious activities. Further, given that the authorities have allegedly continued to inquire about the claimant and allegedly arrested other members, it is reasonable to expect, given the documentary evidence, that an arrest warrant or summons would have been left with the claimant's family.

Given the lack of an arrest warrant/summons and the change in his answer, the panel determines, based on the balance of probabilities that the authorities did not come making inquiries regarding the claimant.

On the basis of the cumulative and important concerns noted above, I conclude that I have insufficient credible or persuasive evidence to demonstrate that the claimant was ever a member of an underground house church in China or was ever detained or sought by the authorities in that country. I find, on a balance of probabilities that he was not a genuine Christian in China, and that he was not a credible witness.

For the aforementioned reasons, and the noted credibility concerns, I also give no weight to any documents purporting to be from China given that the country documentation11 confirms the ease with which individuals may obtain fraudulent copies of police or court documents to corroborate their claims, and that the production and use of fraudulent or counterfeit documents is commonplace in Fujian, particularly amongst those engaged in people smuggling.12

I give no weight to the document purporting to be about the sister's U.S. asylum claim,13 as it is not an original document, nor a certified true copy of an original. In fact, it appears to be a very poor quality photocopy many times removed from any original document, and is virtually illegible. I cannot even begin to read any file number thereon. I have no means to assess if it is genuine or not.

In any event, it tells me nothing about the basis of the sister's claim. If the claimant wished to prove that her claim was related to his, he might well have obtained an affidavit or declaration from her attesting to that, a letter from any U.S. immigration or asylum attorney who represented her, or copies of the documents which she must surely have filed with any American asylum determination system to summarize the basis of her claim. He has had over two and a half years between his arrival in Canada in XXXX 2008 and the conclusion of his oral hearing in July 2011 to do so. He has had benefit of advice from competent legal counsel throughout. The PIF narrative instructions also advise him to attach copies of any documents to support his claim.

The panel does not believe, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is a genuine Christian and, therefore, accordingly the claimant would not necessarily practice Christianity should he return to China today.

On a balance of probabilities, the panel finds that the claimant participated in Christian activities in Toronto in order to substantiate a manufactured claim to be a Convention refugee. As a result, and since the panel is not persuaded that the claimant was a genuine Christian in China prior to coming to Canada, the panel attaches little weight to the photographs and documents from the church.14 The panel is of the view the claimant has obtained these documents to further his claim to be a Convention refugee and a person in need of protection, and that they alone do not corroborate that the claimant actually is or ever was a genuine Christian.

For all the aforementioned reasons, the panel makes a determination, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is not Christian, was not a Christian in China and is not being sought by the PSB in China.

With respect to the documentary evidence,15 Protestant worshippers number at least 20 million people in the official church and between 50 and 70 million in the non-state sanctioned churches. The website of the State Administration for Religious Affairs (SARA) states that family and friends holding meetings at home (as distinct from formal worship in public venues) need not register with the government. However, there were many reports that police and officials of local Religious Affairs Bureaus (RABs) disrupted home worship meetings claiming that participants disturbed neighbours or social order or belonged to an "evil religion."16 Documentation reveals that there is a large discrepancy in the treatment of house churches.17 Urban house churches in some areas limited the size of their meetings to a few dozen individuals. In non-urban areas, some house churches were able to hold meetings that hundreds of individuals attended, with which local authorities did not interfere. Some unregistered religious groups had significant membership, properties, financial resources and networks. House churches faced more risks when their membership grew, they arranged for regular use of facilities for religious activities, or forged links with other unregistered groups or coreligionists overseas.18 Documentation19 also highlights, "Members and leaders of unregistered Protestant groups in China continued to face harassment and harsh punishment, including detention, fines, beatings, confiscation of property, arrest, and mistreatment and torture in custody." The documentation20 also reported that arrests for and harassment of peaceful Protestant religious activity occurred in at least 17 provinces and two municipalities, with the most incidents occurring in Henan, Xinjiang, Shandong, Hebei, and Zhejiang provinces.

With respect to the situation of religious persecution within the claimant's province of Fujian, there is no persuasive information suggesting that religious persecution is occurring for groups that are similar to the claimant's. Although a number of different commentators have reported on the issue of religious persecution in China, one in particular, China Aid Association (CAA), stands out as being a significant source of up-to-date reporting and detailed accounts of harassment and repression of Protestant house churches in China.21 Their report22 identifies five main targets of persecution: House church leaders, house churches in urban areas, forcing churches to quit worship meetings, severe punishment through long term imprisonment and heavy fines on church leaders and believers, and tighter control of the Three-Self Church.

The President of CAA has stated that east coast provinces are generally "more open" with fewer incidents involving Christians reported to CAA. However, the CAA President also stated that this did not necessarily mean there were fewer incidents but rather that they were not reported.23 The CAA reported that one church was demolished in Pingtan in Fujian in 2006.24 The article does not provide context as to the reason the church was destroyed, what denomination it was or when the demolition occurred. Mr. Bob Fu of ChinaAid has also expressed his views to refugee counsel as follows: With specific reference to the provinces Fujian and Guangdong, it is absolutely incorrect to find that there is religious freedom in these provinces. [...] [T]he persecution may come and go and not be totally predictable, but it is always present. Even the very threat of a government crackdown is a method of persecution. The house churches in Fujian and Guangdong, like all of China, face the constant and fearful risk of being closed and its members punished. Certainly, these provinces do not enjoy religious freedom while all other parts of China do not.25

What is clear to the panel is that in China, religious persecution of Protestant "house churches" does occur, however, it is not general in nature. Such factors as whether there are close links with the West, evangelization, membership growth to become large-scale congregations, arrangements for regular use of facilities, whether an individual is a leader, rural or urban areas and location within China are all factors to consider.

The panel is mindful of the caveat that the number of persecution incidents is likely to be much higher because of censorship in communications26 and even considered the possibility that not all information is available to commentators. Considering all these factors, the panel concludes that since there is a significant amount of information detailing very specific examples from areas much more remote and difficult to access than Fujian, which includes not only egregious examples of persecution such as arrests but also other forms of persecution such as fines, short term detentions, confiscation of materials, etc, that it is reasonable for the panel to expect to see persuasive evidence that groups such as the claimant's, which are small and not required to register, are being raided and individuals being jailed or facing other forms of persecution in Fujian province. The documentary evidence persuades the panel, based on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant's unregistered house church was not raided and further supports the determination that the authorities are not making inquiries with respect to the claimant.

With respect to the genuineness of the claimant's Christian faith, even if I were to accept that he is a Christian, - which I specifically do not, - based on any Christian knowledge, any church attendance, or any documentation27 which indicates that he has been baptized, I would refer to documentation,28 which states: Most Christian groups, the majority of which are not members of the PRAs, no longer operated in strict secrecy. Instead, they carried out public activities, including convening seminars, publishing materials, renting space for offices and events, and disseminating information on the Internet.

In addition, previously referred to evidence indicates that between 50 and 70 million individuals belong to the non-state sanctioned churches in China. It is clear that evangelization occurs in China. Given the foregoing evidence of huge numbers of Christian practitioners in the non-state sanctioned churches, documentation which indicates that most Christian groups no longer operated in strict secrecy and carried out public activities and no persuasive evidence that individuals who have evangelized in Fujian province have faced any sort of persecution, the panel determines, that the claimant can return to his home in Fujian province and practice his alleged faith freely and openly.

The panel is supported in this decision, by a recent decision by Mr. Justice Russell.29 While this decision concerns an alleged raid in Guangdong Province, the profile of Fujian province is virtually identical in terms of country document evidence concerning policies and actions in response to membership in underground Christian churches. In reaching his decision, Mr. Justice Russell cited Justice Crampton's decision in Nen Mei Lin, concerning Fujian province, in which the court stated that in the context of the significant detail in the documentation, regarding the dates and locations of arrests and other steps taken to discourage Christian activity in China, it was reasonable for the Board to conclude that, if persecution of members of underground churches occurred in Fujian province, it would have been documented. 30 In addition, Justice Lemieux in Jiang31 noted that the documentary evidence concerning Fujian province indicates there is a minimum of constraints on religious practice, and people generally practice their religion freely.

On the basis of the totality of the evidence, and the cumulative findings, I find that the claimant has not satisfied his burden of establishing a serious possibility that he would be persecuted or that he would be personally subjected to a risk to his life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture, by any authority in the People's Republic of China.

I determine that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. Therefore, the Refugee Protection Division rejects his claim.
